headlines.article_text: Microsoft moves to consolidate its relationships with neoclouds in AI Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Microsoft is looking to shrink the number of neoclouds it counts as partners, according to people familiar with the matter. The company will keep working with some key suppliers while it also builds out its own infrastructure, the sources said. Microsoft has signed deals with half a dozen neoclouds in recent years, including CoreWeave and Nebius. In this article MSFT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 1:16 01:16 Microsoft in process of consolidating neocloud relationships, sources say Squawk on the Street Microsoft is shrinking its roster of neocloud partners as it focuses on work with a few key suppliers and builds out its own data centers, according to people familiar with the matter. The software giant's plans pose another potential challenge for a corner of the artificial intelligence market that's showing signs of strain due to rising borrowing costs, hefty debt loads and concerns about whether the buildout will slow down. Microsoft has forged relationships in recent years with a number of neoclouds, including CoreWeave , Nebius, Chronoscale , IREN , Lambda and Nscale, as well as with Oracle , which is pouring money into building out AI infrastructure. Microsoft is now in the evaluation stage and hasn't decided which neoclouds it will stop using, said two sources, who asked not to be named because the talks are confidential. One of the people said Microsoft wants to prioritize its own data center footprint. Bloomberg reported on the plans earlier. Two people said that Microsoft opted not to renew a deal with Oracle. A Microsoft spokesperson said in an emailed statement that its infrastructure strategy is "built on flexibility and choice." "We combine Microsoft-owned datacenters, leased facilities and strategic partnerships with third-party providers to deliver the capacity our customers need, where and when they need it," the spokesperson said. "We regularly review these investments against customer demand. That includes tracking delivery and adjusting plans as circumstances change." watch now VIDEO 4:13 04:13 Freedom Capital's Paul Meeks: CoreWeave shares may triple Power Lunch The neoclouds have been a turbulent trade on Wall Street in recent weeks as rising interest rates added to fears that many companies have become overly reliant on debt in rushing to build capacity. Shares of CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all down by roughly half over the past month even after rallying on Friday. A recent industry review counted 323 neoclouds , and experts have predicted that many of them won't survive. In its earnings report on Thursday, IREN said it handed over data center capacity to Microsoft in August, but Microsoft requested a networking equipment upgrade that will result in the infrastructure coming online in January or February instead of this year. Microsoft finance chief Amy Hood said on the software company's fiscal first-quarter earnings call in October that some cloud contracts involving graphics processing units were delayed until the first half of 2027, affecting Azure cloud growth. Microsoft reported $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the latest quarter, and said capex spending will accelerate in the second half of the fiscal year. Capital markets 'more selective' CoreWeave and Nebius are both scheduled to report quarterly results next week. IREN shares popped 16% on Friday after the company said AI revenue more than doubled from the prior quarter to $200 million. IREN co-CEO Daniel Roberts told CNBC that there's a "disconnect between what we're seeing in public market and what we're seeing at the customer level." However, he acknowledged the challenge that market conditions present. "Capital markets have become more selective in the last few weeks, and the questions have undoubtedly moved from how big the contract is to whether it can be delivered, financed, and run at a profit," Roberts said on the earnings call. Microsoft has already slashed its work with U.K.-based neocloud Nscale, walking away from a site that it had intended to use in England. Darren Hardman, Microsoft's CEO for the U.K and Ireland, told CNBC in October that the decision had to do with Nscale's ability to get access to electricity. watch now VIDEO 4:18 04:18 Lofty valuations weigh on data center IPOs: Pella Funds CIO Squawk Box Asia The Financial Times reported this week that Microsoft decided against renewing a contract with Nscale in Texas. Nscale filed to go public in mid-September but hasn't updated its prospectus since then. The company said in its IPO filing that it expects Microsoft to be a "significant customer in future periods." Microsoft's big turn to neoclouds came after the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, which led to a surge in demand for GPUs. In looking elsewhere, Microsoft signed up CoreWeave, which was a privately held startup at the time with roots in cryptocurrency mining. When CoreWeave went public last year, it said 62% of its 2024 revenue came from Microsoft. At the time of ChatGPT's release, OpenAI only used Azure. Now the company's cloud suppliers also include Amazon, Cerebras , CoreWeave, Google and Oracle. Microsoft's spokesperson said that its approach to reviewing neocloud investments is "a normal and responsible way to manage large, complex infrastructure projects," and that "the pace of our new agreements reflects what we need today." —CNBC's Kif Leswing contributed to this report. headlines.article_text: OpenAI, Arm, Qualcomm, Box execs react to midterm sell-off concerns Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points A Democratic sweep of Congress and many governorships in the midterm elections Tuesday prompted market fears of a data center slowdown. Stocks sold off sharply Thursday, with major indexes posting their worst day since April 2025, before recovering some of those losses Friday. Executives at some major tech companies reiterated to CNBC the importance of continuing the data center buildout, but expressed skepticism that the worst of the slowdown fears would materialize. Others pointed to strengths in their businesses that would be unaffected by data center concerns. In this article QCOM Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Signage at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, US, on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images As a post-midterm rally Wednesday turned into a steep sell-off Thursday, tech executives sought to look through the notion that potential data center constraints could be catastrophic for their businesses. In response to a Democratic sweep of Congress as well as a sizeable number of state governorships and legislatures in the midterm election Tuesday night, stocks initially rallied Wednesday, posting their best day in more than 18 months as President Trump accepted the blowout results with little fanfare. The tide quickly turned Thursday, however, with stocks selling off sharply as investors feared a potential slowdown in the data center build-out after wins by candidates in favor of data center regulation in states like Texas and the possibility that the artificial intelligence trade may be past its peak. Tech led the sell-off , with the "Magnificent Seven" losing over $1 trillion in aggregate market cap. Stocks recovered some of their losses Friday. Here's how tech executives reacted to the midterms and sell-off threat: Arm CEO Rene Haas watch now VIDEO 3:32 03:32 Arm CEO Rene Haas: We've gained a lot of market share in data center Squawk on the Street Haas characterized the postelection fear as "very, very short term thinking" and not likely to be a major threat to Arm's business in the long term, but said the U.S. must keep investing in the data center build-out before the rest of the world catches up. "If the U.S. hesitates in any way, shape, or form in terms of data center build-out, the rest of the world is ready and willing. There is just huge demand for this capacity," Haas told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Thursday. OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar watch now VIDEO 4:32 04:32 OpenAI will keep investing in AI data centers despite election results, says CFO Sarah Friar Squawk on the Street Friar told CNBC's Sara Eisen Friday that OpenAI will continue investing in data center infrastructure after voters resoundly rejected data centers in their backyards during the midterm election. The company will also focus on community concerns, including electricity. "We will never raise your electricity bill," Friar said. "When I think about the midterms, I need to keep thinking about how do we keep investing to meet that customer demand. It starts early with having built relationships with all of the hyperscalers, and it will continue to mean that we raise capital," Friar said. "If the midterm means more focus on data centers and communities, we're going to keep doing the work to get into those communities and to build trust with them." Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon watch now VIDEO 3:48 03:48 Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon weighs in on data center demand Halftime Report Amon said the anxiety about the future of the data center build-out doesn't pose a significant threat to the chipmaker's business, as data center infrastructure is just one segment. Qualcomm slid 9.49% in Thursday's sell-off before recovering some losses Friday. "The whole market is down, but I think the Qualcomm story is a little bit different," Amon told CNBC's Jon Fortt Thursday. Unlike traditional PC and data center chipmakers, Qualcomm has historically focused on low-power consumption computing. "The story of Qualcomm is what we have done outside that on the data center specific question." Box CEO Aaron Levie watch now VIDEO 3:46 03:46 Box CEO Aaron Levie: Seeing continued acceleration with AI adoption Squawk on the Street Levie told "Squawk on the Street" Thursday that productivity gains meant AI "is clearly going in one direction," but said a tendency for industry messaging to coalesce around "doomerism" can exacerbate the public perception problems AI companies face. "I think it's a little bit easier to rotate it toward maybe the more risk-oriented messages, and that's something that our industry needs to work on clearly. But ultimately, obviously, the consumer needs to see the direct benefit, and that's something that will just take time," said Box's Levie. Lyft CEO David Risher watch now VIDEO 6:50 06:50 Lyft CEO David Risher on Q3 results: Eighth consecutive quarter of double-digit rider growth Squawk Box Risher said the dour market sentiment wasn't concerning for Lyft's business, as consumer sentiment and bookings remained strong. "I wouldn't get too distracted about the short term stuff of what's going on in the market. If I look at the consumer, for example, we just had the biggest Halloween we've ever had," Risher told CNBC's "Squawk Box" Friday. headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: NVDA, MRNA, IONQ, ABNB, FLY Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading. IonQ – The quantum computing stock rose 17% after IonQ lifted its full-year guidance for revenue. The company sees revenue in a range of $505 million to $515 million, topping analysts' estimate for $456.2 million, per FactSet. Firefly Aerospace – The company announced a roughly $1.3 billion agreement with AST SpaceMobile in which it will provide 36 rocket engines and a license to the engine's intellectual property. Firefly surged nearly 30%, while AST SpaceMobile advanced 6%. Microchip Technology – The semiconductor manufacturer tumbled 14% on the back of largely disappointing guidance for the current quarter. Microchip Technology sees third-quarter non-GAAP earnings ranging from 87 cents to 95 cents per share and revenue between $1.573 billion to $1.638 billion. The FactSet consensus estimate called for 94 cents a share and $1.63 billion. Moderna — The vaccine maker rallied 7%. The company smashed third-quarter earnings estimates and raised its outlook for full-year sales growth. Moderna now expects 2026 revenue growth of 15% to 25%, up from previous guidance of no more than 10%. Lam Research — The semiconductor equipment maker surged nearly 9% after the board authorized a $25 billion stock buyback . Five9 — The cloud-based contact-center-as-a-service provider fell more than 17%. Five9 lowered full-year adjusted EPS guidance and announced a $325 million cash acquisition of Level AI. Axon Enterprise — The Taser maker dropped 18% after third-quarter EPS and revenue missed Wall Street estimates, fourth-quarter guidance was weak and it pledged an additional $1.2 billion investment in drone maker Skydio, raising its stake to about 37%. Artificial intelligence and semiconductor stocks — Micron Technology, Sandisk , Marvell Technology, Advanced Micro Devices , Nebius and CoreWeave climbed Friday, recovering ground after Thursday's sharp sell-off amid concerns over potential constraints on AI data-center expansion. Nvidia rebounded more than 3% and returned to positive territory for 2026. Cloudflare — Shares climbed about 12% after guidance for the current quarter topped Street expectations. Cloudflare forecast adjusted earnings of 43 cents a share versus the LSEG consensus for 38 cents, on revenue of $845 million to $846 million, higher than analysts' consensus of $798 million. Iren – The neocloud provider jumped 19% after fiscal first-quarter revenue of $228 million grew from $137 million the prior quarter. More than $4 billion in annual recurring revenue projected to arrive in 2026 has been delayed until at least January 2027. Iren has been battered in the latest rout of AI-focused stocks, dropping 31% in the past week. Airbnb — The online lodging marketplace jumped 11% after third-quarter earnings of $3.16 per share topped analysts' consensus estimate of $2.85. Revenue of $4.87 billion beat the Street's $4.75 billion estimate, LSEG data showed. Atlassian — Shares dropped more than 14% after the supplier of team collaboration and productivity software showed year-over-year data center revenue growth expected to decline approximately 14% in the fiscal second quarter ending in December, and 16% in the fiscal year ending next June. JFrog — The software company soared 35% after raising full-year guidance. JFrog sees adjusted earnings ranging from $1.14 to $1.16 per share on revenue of $680 million to $682 million. The outlook trounced FactSet consensus estimates of 98 cents a share and $651.9 million. DraftKings — The online sports betting platform tumbled 27%. DraftKings posted a wider-than-expected third-quarter loss of 94 cents per share, worse than the 39 cent loss analysts polled by LSEG anticipated. Revenue of $1.33 billion fell short of the $1.40 billion estimate. Sportsbook revenue totaled $784 million, missing the $811.8 million StreetAccount consensus estimate. Lyft — The ridesharing company fell almost 5%. Third-quarter revenue of $1.82 billion trailed the FactSet consensus among analysts for $1.92 billion, while fourth-quarter guidance for bookings came in at $5.74 billion to $5.94 billion versus the FactSet consensus of $5.81 billion. — CNBC's Nick Wells, Darla Mercado and Scott Schnipper contributed reporting
